content: Aboulia, also known as Abulia, is a neurological condition characterized by a lack of willpower or initiative. The term originates from the Greek word αβουλία, which translates to non-will. Patients with aboulia are unable to act or make decisions independently. The severity of this condition can vary, ranging from subtle manifestations to profound impairments. Aboulia can result from various types of brain injuries that lead to changes in personality. These injuries may include dementing illnesses, traumatic brain injuries, or intracerebral hemorrhages (strokes). It is particularly associated with strokes that cause diffuse damage to the right hemisphere of the brain. In stroke patients, aboulia can complicate rehabilitation efforts, as affected individuals may show a lack of interest in performing tasks, such as walking, even when they are physically capable of doing so. It is important to distinguish aboulia from apraxia. In apraxia, a brain-injured patient has difficulty understanding the movements required to perform a motor task, despite not having any paralysis that would prevent them from completing the task. Apraxia can also result in a lack of initiation of activity, but the underlying mechanism differs from that of aboulia. In patients with progressive dementia, aboulia can significantly impact feeding behaviors. For example, these patients may continue to chew or hold food in their mouths for extended periods without swallowing. This behavior is often more noticeable after they have consumed part of their meal and no longer feel a strong appetite. To address this issue, caregivers can introduce sweet or salty foods later in the meal to stimulate interest and encourage oral intake. However, it is essential for caregivers to ensure that the patient’s mouth is cleared of food after each meal to prevent complications.
